course_details.Overview of class: Before Tolstoy and Dostoevsky came three canonical 19th century Russian writers: Pushkin, Gogol, and Lemontov. In this early era, Russia was heavily in dialogue with Western European culture, which introduced Russia to a new genre of writing- the novel. Stepped in poetry, the gothic and the Romantic, these writers' groundbreaking works resounded through the generations that followed. We explore the history, culture, and society that produced these long-studied classic of Russian literature.

course_details.Overview of class: In LING 222/SLAVIC 222 Language, Politics, and Identity (co-listed classes) students will examine and analyze political and identity issues in terms of the languages and dialects of the Balkans (particularly: Albanian, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Croatian, Macedonian, Romani, and Serbian). Topics to be covered include: linguistic nationalism, language laws, rights of minority languages, language discrimination, language and religion, alphabet issues, language and dialect as ethnic identity, standard language, and others. This course will introduce the student to some of the key issues that have plagued the Balkans in the past and continue to shape its future.
course_details.Registration Requirements: This course fulfills either an Area IV, Historical Studies, Distribution Requirement or Area V, Ethics and Values, Distribution Requirement, students may choose with Distribution Requirement.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
Describe the major historical events and figures within the Balkans, relevant to our sociolinguistic lens, from antiquity to modernity that have shaped key arguments about nationalism, language, and language-related social practices.
Intercept secondary sources (written histories, historical atlases of the Balkans, and other scholarly works) to acquire knowledge of the impact of historical developments and factors on the emergence and development of literary languages.
Apply a sociolinguistic social justice lens to these historical developments and factors, including the ancient civilizations (Illyria and Thrace) and major empires in the Balkans (Roman, Greek, Habsburg, and especially Ottoman), the decline of the Ottoman Empire and influx of Romantic nationalism, Communism, the Yugoslav Wars, and the rise of the European Union.
Analyze primary sources to discover the forms, effects, and causes of linguistic nationalism through the historical context. Primary texts include the 1850 Literary Agreement in Vienna, the 1954 Novi Sad Agreement, the 1967 Declaration on the Name and Position of the Croatian Literary Language, the 1974 revised Yugoslav Constitution, the 2017 Declaration on the Common Language, the 1944 Presidium of Anti-fascist Assembly of the National Liberation of Macedonia Announcement of Instruction in Schools in the Macedonian Language, the 1945 Foundation of the Macedonian Literary Language, and the 1945 People's Government of Macedonia Decree on the Macedonian Alphabet.
Reflect on the historical construction of ethnicity and nationalism and the roles these play in attitudes towards and policies concerning linguistic varieties (languages and dialects) and how they have changed over time. Particular attention will be given to the Ottoman Empire's administrative community structure, millet, in contrast to the Western Romantic nationalism entering the Balkans in the 19th century through external Western powers. Students will examine how these competing frameworks shaped and reshaped ethnicity and nationalism, ultimately contributing to forms of linguistic prejudice that have characterized the Balkans since the nineteenth century.
Recognize the significant symbolic role that language plays in politics and identity by describing and critiquing models of language policy within the Balkans ranging from total support and flourishing to attempting to kill and erase languages (and, consequently, peoples and cultures). Recognize the complexity of ethical issues associated with language politics and describe possible improvements to linguistic policy models based on the Balkan cases.
Identify linguistic prejudice through the myths and presuppositions about language (e.g., "speakers of African American English are verbally deprived"; "some languages are not good enough"; "everyone has an accent except me;" "French is a logical language"; "the meanings of words should not be allowed to change").
Discuss ways to prevent the perpetuation of linguistic prejudice and to promote linguistic justice and diversity within societies, particularly in contexts involving minority languages, colonization, genocide, and war.
Define foundational concepts of sociolinguistics/linguistic anthropology, using the Balkans as our primary case study and drawing comparisons with parallel US situations. Concepts include dialect continuum, language and identity, diglossia, alphabet reform, polycentric language models, language loss, language codification, language planning, and models of minority languages.
Discuss the vast and complex diachronic and synchronic multilayered diversity of the Balkans. Learn the countries and regions (historical, current, and non-existent, e.g., Greater Albania, non-territorial communities of Roma and Jews), major peoples and religions, and the names and genetic classifications of the major linguistic varieties (languages and dialects) while exhaming how these categories and systems of thought and speech have been constructed over time and space.
Communicate effectively about language policy and language politics in the Balkans and their historical development, expressing ideas thoughtfully and clearly in both oral and written forms.
Practice and improve group-work skills, including developing intercultural competence, sharing and supporting expertise, managing conflict within groups, planning and managing time effectively, giving and receiving constructive feedback, strengthening communication and listening skills, improving turn-taking practices, and holding oneself and others accountable.

course_info.course_name: The Apocalypse: End Times in Russian Literature an

course_details.Topic: The Apocalypse: End Times in Russian Literature an
course_details.Overview of class:
Since at least the time of Ivan the Terrible, Russians have demonstrated a distinct obsession with the end of history, not just to understand and predict such an end, but to live in it, either by preventing or hastening its disclosure. Similarly for many Russian writers and philosophers, the apocalypse has been a point of orientation as much as disorientation. The end of time acts as conceptual deadline, and therefore as a stimulus to moral, aesthetic, and metaphysical reflection and clarity. It forces one to see one's ideas to their conclusion, to confront contradictions and tensions that are easy to ignore amid the commotion of life. These contrasts include: good and evil, life and death, immorality and morality, truth and falsehood, faith and nihilism, fear and love, God and human, Christ and Antichrist, God and Devil. The apocalypse may make such dialectics inescapable, but parsing them will remain ever more paradoxical and fascinating.

Focusing on Russian literature but with crucial forays into philosophical and religious thought, this course surveys how Russian creative writers and thinkers have invoked the paradoxes and narratives of the apocalypse to formulate a redemptive image of the world and of the human being, even as their stories and essays will readily admit that the impulse towards "redemption" can be highjacked for the purposes of evil at an individual and at a national level. The final part of the course will consider the resurgence of interest in the apocalypse and the Antichrist both in Russia and the West, especially the reception and influence of Russian apocalypticism on the West.

In this course, we will read novels and short-stories by authors such as Alexander Pushkin, Nikolai Gogol, Fyodor Dostoevsky, Leo Tolstoy, Mikhail Bakhtin, and, most recently, by Eugene Vodolazkin. We will also read philosophical essays by thinkers such as Vladimir Solovyov, Nikolai Berdiaev, and Sergei Bulgakov.

course_details.Overview of class: This course will survey Polish film (all subtitled) from its earliest beginnings at the turn of the 20th century to the present day. We will begin by watching Poland's earliest talkies and films of the interwar period before discussing the Holocaust and Stalinism and its "thaw" on film during the communist era. From there, we will discuss the Polish Film School and the Cinema of Morality Anxiety. Further, we will analyze themes of absurdism and the subversive, and later examine teh changes forms, subjects, and elements of films in post-1989 Poland. We will watch films by such directors as Juliusz Gardan, Stanisław Bareja, Andrzej Wajda, Wanda Jakubowska, Aleksander Ford, Kryszstof Kieślowski, and Paweł Pawlikowski.

Martina Kerlova (Ph.D. in Modern History, Charles University, Prague; M.A. in German Studies, Charles University) is a Professor of Instruction in the Department of German and the Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures. She has published and presented on Austrian and German literature and language teaching methodology. Her academic interests include Central European literature, film, history, and languages, and their Anglo-American connections. She coordinates the Intermediate German language program and serves as Director of Slavic Languages. She also works as a translator.
course_details.Overview of class: This course examines Prague, one of the most beautiful and culturally vibrant cities in Europe. The city's magnificent streets and buildings both conceal and reveal a past full of multiethnic coexistence and interethnic conflict. The course follows the development of Prague over the past century from the interwar multicultural, democratic city to the postwar homogeneous, communist community, and ultimately to its present open and capitalist incarnation. The goal of our course will be to understand how Prague's various communities built the city and its culture(s) and how they struggled to control it. We will read and watch a range of literary and historical sources, including the story of the Golem and writings by Václav Havel, and Franz Kafka.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
- To consider the productive (as well as the destructive) consequences of interethnic strife and political repression
- To investigate how cultural producers and consumers respond to divisive pressures from within and censorious pressures from without.
- To understand the contingent and malleable nature of national and other identities.
- To gain familiarity with the city of Prague and its culture

course_details.Overview of class:
Is Kashubian (Cassubian; kaszëbsczi jãzëk; or in Polish język kaszubski) a dialect of Polish or a separate West Slavic language closely related to Polish? In Ukraine are Russian-speaking Ukrainians Ukrainians? Are German-speaking Turks in Germany Germans? Are Sorbian-speaking Germans in Germany Germans? Are Czech and Slovak the same or different languages? In Estonia if you only speak Russian can you be Estonian? This course explores the deep connections among language, identity, and power in a region shaped by shifting borders, political upheavals, linguistic diversity, and cultural and dialectal continua. We'll examine how language is used as a tool of identity and nation marking and building, resistance, and exclusion to the point of often denying identity. Topics to be examined include: language myths, language vs. dialect, language policies, language planning, language and identity, language rights.

A final paper and no final exam is required for the course. Assignment drafts of the final paper build towards the course grade.

course_details.Overview of class: This course examines queer literature, art, and politics across Poland, Russia, and Ukraine from the late Soviet era to the present. Together, we trace how shifting political regimes shape gender and sexuality. We begin with the communist period of surveillance and underground networks. Next, we examine the transition to capitalism, focusing on the clash between local "Soviet queens" and global gays. Finally, we explore contemporary struggles, from Pussy Riot's protest art against Putin to queer military participation in Ukraine. We also analyze queer resistance against today's "anti-gender" movements and the strategies Eastern European feminist collectives have offered. Through the study of fiction, poetry, performance art, and documentary film, students will develop critical tools to engage with the urgent aesthetic and political questions defining Slavic queer life.
course_details.Class Notes: Previous knowledge of Eastern European cultures is helpful but not required. All texts will be available in English translation.

course_details.Overview of class:
This seminar will examine the school and theory of Russian Formalism, which influenced and informed many developments in the 20th century literary and art theory, from Prague Linguistic Circle through Structuralism and Semiotics. Along with the detailed study of the critical and theoretical essays by such adherents of Formalism as Victor Shklovsky, Roman Jacobson, Yuri Tynianov, Boris Eikhenbaum, et al., we will be exploring the major works of Russian modernism and avant-garde in literature and film through the methodological approach of Formalist theory. Special focus on the issues of Formalism and Marxism, Formalism and History, and the interconnections between culture and politics of the time.
Discussion and presentations in English.
